headline: AI agents sweep i18n leaks, reducing 300 candidates to 60 real bugs
summary: A team used four parallel AI agents and AST-based filtering to uncover 60 critical internationalization bugs, including Stripe webhook emails sent in Japanese to English-paying users for months.
details: For large bilingual applications, finding hardcoded foreign language strings is a persistent challenge. A simple grep often yields thousands of hits, with most being harmless entries in translation tables, already-branched code, or comments, obscuring the actual leaks.

To address this, a team deployed four parallel AI investigation agents combined with Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-based false-positive filtering. This advanced pipeline efficiently processed approximately 300 initial candidates, ultimately identifying 60 genuine internationalization bugs.

The AI agents operated independently, each assigned a different code surface area and given the same prompt to enumerate user-facing hardcoded Japanese strings. This parallel execution significantly reduced wall-clock time and improved coverage by offering multiple perspectives on the problem.

After the initial AI scan, the merged report still contained around 300 candidates, too many for manual review. A Python script leveraging the `ast` module was then used to mechanically check for language branching around Japanese literals, effectively filtering out most false positives.

The most impactful discovery among the 60 real leaks was that all four Stripe webhook emails (purchase complete, renewal, payment failed, plan change) were hardcoded to Japanese. This meant English-paying users had been receiving critical notifications in Japanese for an extended period.

The fix involved implementing a one-function language inference from the Stripe event, which then branched the email subject and body content. Additionally, `mb_language` settings were corrected to ensure English subjects were UTF-8 Base64 encoded, preventing ISO-2022-JP encoding that could raise spam scores.

Further consolidation efforts included centralizing all language detection into a single helper function, `resolve_request_lang()`, used across various API endpoints. A unified English plan-name table, `PLAN_NAMES_EN`, was also established as a single point of truth for plan names.

Other remaining hardcoded leaks found in core files like `core/license.py`, `core/key_perms.py`, desktop launchers, and landing-page APIs received similar treatment. Each was refactored to extract small helpers, branch on language, and route through a single entry point.

This comprehensive approach, combining parallel AI agents with AST-based filtering, transformed the vague anxiety of hidden hardcoded strings into a quantifiable and manageable problem. The pipeline now allows for on-demand assessment of internationalization integrity.

headline_marked: [[Real-time arrhythmia detection at the edge]] using TinyML on ESP32 for raw ECG analysis
headline: Real-time arrhythmia detection at the edge using TinyML on ESP32 for raw ECG analysis
summary: This approach moves intelligence from the cloud to the device, ensuring low-latency detection of arrhythmias while keeping sensitive medical data private and on-device.
details: Wearable health technology is advancing by moving intelligence from the cloud to the edge. This tackles latency, privacy, and battery life concerns by processing data locally on devices.

By leveraging TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers and the versatile ESP32, raw electrocardiogram (ECG) data can be processed directly on the device. This enables real-time abnormality detection with minimal delay.

The process involves capturing high-frequency analog ECG signals, cleaning them, and feeding them into a quantized Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Models are typically trained using databases like MIT-BIH Arrhythmia.

A crucial step for ESP32 deployment is Post-Training Quantization, converting 32-bit float models to 8-bit integer (INT8). This reduces model size by 4x and significantly speeds up inference with minimal accuracy loss.

Moving from prototype to production introduces challenges like signal noise from muscle movement (EMG) and power consumption. Robust noise-cancellation algorithms and efficient memory management are key for TinyML deployments.

Raw ECG data requires digital Bandpass Filters (typically 0.5Hz to 40Hz) to remove baseline wander and high-frequency noise. These can be implemented as simple IIR filters in C++ to maintain low computational overhead on the ESP32.

Deploying a CNN on an ESP32 for real-time ECG analysis represents a significant step towards decentralized healthcare. This method enhances user privacy and reduces the load on central infrastructure.
